title: Ariana Grande Debuts at No. 1 on Album Chart With ‘Petal,’ Earning Her Best First-Week Numbers in Seven Years
description: Ariana Grande has earned her seventh No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 chart with “Petal,” which bows in the top spot with 295,000 equivalent album u
body:
Ariana Grande has earned her seventh No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 chart with “Petal,” which bows in the top spot with 295,000 equivalent album units, her best opening-week figure this decade.

	“Petal” and its songs and videos have been the topic of considerable conversation, and any controversy seems to have only helped the album find more traction. The first-week number is the best Grande has had for any album since 2019. It’s a sizable uptick from the 227,000 that her previous album, “Eternal Sunshine,” opened with in 2024. It also outdoes the first weeks for “Sweetener” and “Positions.” Among all of her eight studio albums, only “Thank U, Next” had a bigger opening, with 360,000 units in 2019.
	

	Of the 295,000 units Grande registered for the week, album sales were responsible for 168,000 of those, adding up to her second-best sales week ever, according to Billboard. (Only “My Everything” in 2014 had a bigger sales week for Grande.) A sizable 96,000 of those units were sold on vinyl. The new album’s on-demand streams added up to 128.83 million, translating to 126,000 SEA units.


	Apart from Grande’s entree on top, there was little difference in this week’s top 10 from last week’s top 10 — with the exception of Charli xcx’s latest, “Music, Fashion, Film,” dropping out of the top 10, after debuting last week at No. 3 with 75,000 units. (How far Charli fell isn’t yet known; Billboard only releases the top 10 on Sunday, with the remainder of the Billboard 200 being published Monday.)

	Morgan Wallen and Noah Kahan remain the only artists to each have two albums in the top 10 at present.
	

	The other nine albums following Grande’s in the top 10: Wallen’s “I’m the Problem,” which was No. 1 last week, falling a spot to No. 2, with 75,000 units; Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” down one slot to No. 3 with 74,000; and Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” at No. 4, Kahan’s “The Great Divide” at No. 5, Drake’s “Iceman” at No. 6, Wallen’s “One Thing at a Time” at No. 7, Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” at No. 8, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” at No. 9 and Kahan’s “Stick Season” at No. 10.

	Grande has an excellent shot at being No. 1 for at least one more week after this, as well, given the lack of newly arriving superstar releases. The most notable releases from this past Friday that may impact the next chart came from Role Model and Ravyn Lenae, who aren’t likely to topple Grande. The week after that, she might face competition from Phoebe Bridgers’ first new album in six years.

	“Petal” had the sixth-best opening so far in 2026. The leaders in big debuts have been BTS’ “Arirang” (with 641,000 equivalent album units in its debut), Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad…” (485,000 opening units), Drake’s “Iceman” (463,000), Harry Styles’ “Kiss All the Time. Disco Occasionally” (430,000) and Kahan’s “The Great Divide” (389,000).

schema.headline: Ariana Grande Debuts at No. 1 on Album Chart With ‘Petal,’ Earning Her Best First-Week Numbers in Seven Years

title: ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Cinematographer, Editor and Star Jack Haven Break Down Little Death’s Bloody One-Take Dance
description: When “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” director Jane Schoenbrun described their vision for the bloody one-take sequence in which Little Death (
body:
When “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” director Jane Schoenbrun described their vision for the bloody one-take sequence in which Little Death (Jack Haven) massacres an entire summer camp — all set to Counting Crows’ 1996 rock ballad “A Long December” — they said it should feel like a Michael Bay movie.

	“That’s the one part of the movie where it doesn’t have a filthy old print look to it,” cinematographer Eric Yue tells Variety. “It should feel cool and not in another era’s language, so we built upon that.”
	

	In “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” a young queer filmmaker (Hannah Einbinder) travels to the cabin of a reclusive movie star (Gillian Anderson) in order to convince her to revitalize her career with a remake of “Camp Miasma,” which, in the world of the film, is its own “Friday the 13th”-style slasher franchise.


	The bloody-as-hell sequence comes about halfway through the film, upending everything we’ve seen before. It features a series of hidden cuts and merges three locations together from the camp shoreline to the counselor’s lounge. Everything was carefully timed and choreographed to “A Long December,” including Little Death stabbing people every time the lyrics landed on the word “Hollywood.”

	Since Schoenbrun was able to secure the rights to the song early in production, the crew had a significant amount of time to coordinate the film’s most ambitious sequence. Using an iPhone Steadicam to practice, the crew marked out where each of the beats needed to happen in the space.

	“Jane is definitely a master of pop culture recontextualizations and cool, jarring combinations with a very deep-cut cinephile thing,” editor Graham Mason says.
	

	Yue, who previously worked on “I Saw the TV Glow,” collaborated closely with Schoenbrun to storyboard the sequence for over 100 hours. While much of it was done practically, the sequence also required heavy VFX from the North Vancouver-based agency Niche — specifically to enhance the blood and exploding bodies.

	“Jane would describe it as a Zack Snyder ‘300’ kind of blood,” Yue says. “The blood was meant to feel playful. It wasn’t something that makes you gag like, ‘Oh, this is too realistic.’ Every component of this was fun, including the snow, which isn’t necessarily realistic. Everything is heightened.”



	

	



	The only 16mm shot of the film is of Billy (Anderson) looking directly at the camera before the film flares out and switches to the Little Death oner. The crew rented a Bolex camera to get this added “lift” right before the big sequence, Yue explains. “We almost feel like something has been reversed.”

	Heavy stuntwork was required on Haven’s part; they had to wear a heavy rig with a smaller 35mm camera attached while doing the dance. “So every single time we did a take, we’d have to reload, and that was physically taxing on Jack,” Yue says, explaining that it took around seven or eight takes to nail the ballet-like sequence.

	Haven, who also starred in “I Saw the TV Glow,” says that Schoenbrun “knew” Little Death lived inside them.

	“They knew that I could represent this very specific experience of a character, which is someone who lives outside of the human but is this pure expression,” Haven says. “Jane knows that I am really transformative as a performer and I can change my body to a character. We say that I’m a creature that they can morph.”

	The dance was choreographed by stunt coordinator Maja Aro. “The stunt performers were throwing themselves against the wall when the camera would turn, dropping to the ground. So it’s this very tightly choreographed ballet,” Haven says.

	“And then Jane worked in the moment [at the end] where we see Little Death’s eyes and some sexy little rubbing blood on the face,” Haven adds. “My god, that’s his favorite thing!”



	

	



	In addition to practicing at home with a spear to get the slasher movements just right, Haven would also send Schoenbrun videos with different Little Death walk options. “As a person, I’m kind of small, so it needed to be something sort of intimidating. It ended up being a Michael Myers and ‘Terminator’ cross of stillness with an immovable force. So I had that vocabulary going into it,” Haven says.
	

	“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” as a film, interrogates the legacy of the “Camp Miasma” slasher universe and how it resonates for queer viewers, mainly Kris (Einbinder). The Little Death sequence is particularly notable, then, because it suddenly forces the viewer to grapple with the perspective of the franchise villain.

	Yue explains: “That is a concrete example where we watch Little Death, we kind of go into his helmet, now we’re becoming the POV of Little Death and then we come out of the body and watch. At the end, we almost feel like the camera is getting stabbed in some way.”

	He commends Haven’s performance, adding: “During so much of the film, Jack’s wearing their helmet and we can’t see their face. But the physicality they bring to it is so unique.”

	Thematically, the sequence is also about identifying with The Other, which is reinforced through the way the perspective evolves. “There is a component where we also feel and empathize with Little Death in a way. Sometimes the killer in these horror films, we actually don’t understand their perspective,” Yue says. “There’s this catharsis here.”

	Another scene in the film with a distinctly Schoenbrun touch is the opening title sequence, set to an R.E.M. cover of “Night Swimming.” It lays out the entire “Camp Miasma” lore without a single line of expositional dialogue — from newspaper clippings, VHS tapes, DVDs to merch. And it was filmed on the last day of production.

	Like the Little Death oner, it required extensive cooperation with Schoenbrun’s closest collaborators.

	Mason recalls that from the very beginning, Schoenbrun’s script read: “This movie will have an awesome opening title sequence!”

	“It tells the rise and fall of this horror movie franchise through all this ephemera,” Mason says. “It’s ambitious and asks a lot of the viewer right off the bat. It’s sort of saying, ‘Pay closer attention. This movie will reward your attentiveness.'”

	When testing the film, Mason and Schoenbrun realized they could plant some extra exposition. “Like describing Kris as a Sundance wonderkid and showing a fake TMZ article that’s saying, ‘Billy is horror’s great recluse,'” Mason says.

	The opening title sequence, of course, is filled with plenty of Easter eggs over the course of the 45-year-old franchise, from the director listed as the original “Camp Miasma” director, to a board game that’s actually playable, to hidden glimpses of Little Death’s costume in the arcade game. Additionally, all the articles written about the old “Camp Miasma” films were fully fleshed-out, canonically accurate pieces.
	

	Mason says that Schoenbrun approached “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” as if they were just making a movie with some friends before bouncing those ideas off against the bigger resources of VFX and craftspeople.

	He says of both Little Death’s dance and the opening title sequence: “Jane wanted the film to have this handmade, DIY, almost outsider art quality.”

	“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is currently playing in select theaters from Mubi.

schema.headline: ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Cinematographer, Editor and Star Jack Haven Break Down Little Death’s Bloody One-Take Dance

title: Olivia Wilde Calls ‘The Invite’ the ‘Most Incredible’ Experience of Her Life: ‘It Was the Highlight of My Career’
description:
Olivia Wilde brought “The Invite” to Locarno.

	“I’m in shock. This is overwhelming and exciting,” she told the audience at Piazza Grande, which rep
body:
Olivia Wilde brought “The Invite” to Locarno.

	“I’m in shock. This is overwhelming and exciting,” she told the audience at Piazza Grande, which reportedly has one of the world’s largest cinema screens. 

	“This is the European premiere of ‘The Invite’ and it’s the first time – and probably the only time – it will be seen on a screen this big. I can’t tell you how much this means. I’m so grateful that you came tonight.”
	

	Youn can watch the video here: 




	Earlier that day, Wilde had admitted that she had fought for the film to be released theatrically. 

	“I have the benefit of hearing from audiences and hearing how cathartic they have found it to laugh at some of these things and to laugh with strangers,” she said during a press conference at the fest. 

	“If you don’t fight for it, they ‘bribe’ you to not take theatrical. But we were really lucky that our financier gave me the opportunity to make this decision, which is something I don’t take lightly.”

	The gamble paid off – Variety reported that “The Invite” has become a “rare hit summer comedy.” Owen Gleiberman praised the film in his review, calling it a “bravura dinner-party dramedy that’s like ‘Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?’ redone as vintage Woody Allen.”

	Wilde also said the film was a “love letter to so many of the filmmakers that made us want to do this. People like Cassavetes, Mike Nichols, Mazursky, Woody Allen, Billy Wilder, Nora Ephron and Agnès Varda.” 
	

	“They introduced us to the idea of independent cinema allowing for real vulnerability.”

	It stars Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton as two couples who meet for a dinner party, only for one relationship to implode. 

	“This film is the most incredible experience of my life because it was the most collaborative project,” she noted. 

	“It was workshopped by the cast and our incredible screenwriters, and it’s a remake of an extraordinary Spanish film [‘Sentimental’], which was also interpreted as Swiss-German, French, Italian and South Korean versions. It’s an international story, and what you will watch tonight is our offering and our interpretation. It’s our attempt to be as honest with the audience as we possibly could. For me, it was the highlight of my career.”

	While the story goes into some dark places, humor plays a significant role. 

	“First and foremost, it’s a comedy,” stated Wilde.

	“Even the most tragic things in life, and the way we ultimately overcome them, is by recognizing they didn’t just happen to us. There’s something about understanding the universal experience that removes shame and allows things to be funny — and survivable.” 

	It might be about heartbreak, but it’s still “supposed to be a good time.” 

	“I hope you guys are not too hot and that you can laugh together. The most rewarding thing about this has been hearing audiences laugh together, and maybe cry. You are allowed to cry if you want to. But it is designed to be something that will bring you joy,” she said. 

	“I can’t tell you how much we laughed when we were making it. It was the most hilarious experience. We have to find the hilarity inside the tragic. It’s the only way.”

schema.headline: Olivia Wilde Calls ‘The Invite’ the ‘Most Incredible’ Experience of Her Life: ‘It Was the Highlight of My Career’

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Is Christopher Nolan’s Highest-Grossing Movie Ever With $1.1 Billion and Imax’s Biggest Release of All Time With $289 Million
description: “The Odyssey” has notched two major box office milestones over the weekend. The big-budget adaptation of Homer’s original epic is officially Christo
body:
“The Odyssey” has notched two major box office milestones over the weekend. The big-budget adaptation of Homer’s original epic is officially Christopher Nolan‘s biggest movie ever, with $1.1 billion, ranking ahead of 2012’s “The Dark Knight Rises” with $1.08 billion, not adjusted for inflation. And the sword-and-sandal adventure is Imax’s highest-grossing release of all time with $289 million, overtaking 2009’s “Avatar” with $271 million, not adjusted for inflation.
	

	It’s currently the second-biggest movie of the year behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” with $1.67 billion, as well as the second-highest-grossing R-rated release of all time, following 2024’s “Deadpool and Wolverine” with $1.3 billion.

	These benchmarks are significant because “The Odyssey” isn’t close to winding down its theatrical run. So far, the R-rated movie has generated $461 million domestically and $643 million internationally for a combined tally of $1.1 billion globally. That’s after collecting a staggering $110 million globally, including $79 million overseas and $31.5 million domestically, in its fourth weekend of release. And “The Odyssey” doesn’t open in China, the second-biggest moviegoing market, until Aug. 14.


	Nolan, the most bankable director of his generation, became a box office draw through hits like “The Dark Knight” trilogy, “Inception,” “Dunkirk” and “Interstellar.” His movies have grossed a combined $7 billion globally, including three — “The Odyssey,” 2009’s “The Dark Knight” and “The Dark Knight Rises” — that crossed the coveted billion-dollar mark. Meanwhile, 2023’s “Oppenheimer,” the filmmaker’s first Oscar-best picture winner, was pretty close with $975 million, a remarkable tally for a three-hour historical biopic.
	

	“A singular filmmaker with the international following of Christopher Nolan is uniquely fit to adapt Homer’s ancient poem, which is one of the most influential and well-known stories in the world,” said Veronika Kwan Vandenberg, Universal’s president of international distribution. “’The Odyssey’ is a global epic that has resonated with audiences everywhere with its massive scope and uncompromising vision.”

	“The Odyssey,” starring Matt Damon as the Greek king Odysseus, is notable as the first feature shot entirely with Imax cameras. (Other tentpoles incorporate Imax’s technology for select sequences.) In North America, “The Odyssey” has generated $147.3 million in Imax to stand as the company’s biggest domestic release to date. International markets have accounted for $141.8 million — and that’s before the film lands in China, where Imax has roughly 800 screens. Already, “The Odyssey” has generated $6.3 million from preview screenings in China.

	Meanwhile Imax 70mm formats — otherwise known as Nolan’s preferred viewing experience — have contributed $37.5 million from just 41 locations globally, representing 14% of the company’s total grosses. Given the scarcity of 70mm auditoriums, many of those locations are sold out through September.

	“We had the very highest of hopes for ‘The Odyssey’ from the start,” says Imax’s CEO Richard Gelfond. “But it somehow continues to exceed them, and its historic performance is headlining what we expect will be our best year ever at the global box office.”

schema.headline: ‘The Odyssey’ Is Christopher Nolan’s Highest-Grossing Movie Ever With $1.1 Billion and Imax’s Biggest Release of All Time With $289 Million

title: ‘Five Nights at Freddy’s’ to Open Real Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza Location in 2027
description: “Five Nights at Freddy’s” and New Jersey entertainment and retail center American Dream will open a real-life Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza location in Eas
body:
“Five Nights at Freddy’s” and New Jersey entertainment and retail center American Dream will open a real-life Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza location in East Rutherford, N.J., in 2027.

	Based on the “Five Nights at Freddy’s” franchise, the immersive restaurant experience is a functional reimagining of the game’s location, designed in collaboration with IP holder ScottGames.

	The pizzeria will be a quick-service dining experience featuring two animatronic stage shows: the Main Stage with Freddy and the Fazbear Band, and the Pirate Cove with Foxy the Pirate. Fans can eat, play arcade games, watch an animatronic show and participate in survival horror multiplayer game experiences. 
	

	“The only way this experience succeeds is if it’s created by a team that knows ‘Five Nights at Freddy’s’ inside and out,” said Atreyu Alcantar, creative manager, licensing & location-based entertainment at American Dream and creative lead for the attraction. “The animatronic show has to be authentic. The food has to be high quality. And above all else, we’re not building a set that looks like Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza – we’re building Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza. This experience will immerse longtime fans in the world they’ve imagined for years while welcoming an entirely new audience to discover it for the first time.”


	“Five Nights at Freddy’s” originated as a video game series and has since expanded into novels, graphic novels and films. Created by Scott Cawthon, the game’s story arcs typically follow a character attempting to survive attacks from homicidal animatronic characters. The locations are connected to the fictional pizza restaurant franchise Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza.
	

	American Dream’s other attractions include DreamWorks Water Park, Nickelodeon Universe Theme Park, Sesame Street Learn & Play, Legoland Discovery Center and Sea Life Aquarium.

schema.headline: ‘Five Nights at Freddy’s’ to Open Real Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza Location in 2027

title: The Blockbuster Mentality Is Back, Baby!
description: The suits of Hollywood are used to big numbers. That’s how they roll. But the record-setting opening weekend of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” isn’t so
body:
The suits of Hollywood are used to big numbers. That’s how they roll. But the record-setting opening weekend of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” isn’t something that happens every day, or every year — more like once a decade. Domestically, the film enjoyed the biggest opening weekend in movie history. And while it had to take No. 2, behind “Avengers: Endgame,” when it came to international grosses, it’s still a staggering fact to consider that “Brand New Day” made nearly $1 billion, the benchmark of triumph for any contemporary blockbuster…in just 72 hours. It now has a chance to become the first movie to hit $1 billion domestically, and the first to reach $3 billion globally. These aren’t just numbers that stun and dazzle, that inspire a studio’s board members to order cases of Krug. These are numbers to get high on, to shoot up on. You may ask: How could the blockbuster mentality be back…if it never went away? Let’s just say that the blockbuster mentality waxes and wanes. The key word in the phrase is not, of course, blockbuster. It­’s mentality — a set of thoughts and attitudes and impulses that coalesce into a state-of-mind that supremely prioritizes the making of ginormous-grossing motion pictures. The blockbuster mentality has a rational side. Hollywood is a business, and that business is successful when movies become huge hits. That’s been true since the dawn of the film industry. But the blockbuster mentality also has an irrational side, an irrational exuberance. I would liken it to the experience described by addicts of the first time they get high on crack cocaine. Many have said that that first high is the greatest sensation of their lives, and they have a compulsion to keep chasing it. And that, in its way, is the feeling that was launched 50 years ago by “Jaws” and “Star Wars.” Flash forward, and it’s the feeling the opening weekend of “Brand New Day” can give you. $1 billion in 72 hours. A number like that can become a fix the industry never stops chasing. The Hollywood we know has been built on blockbusters, on sequels and franchises, on IP, on corporate escapist popcorn. And in 2026, a business that looked, for a few years there, like it might be enduring an existential meltdown (COVID, the streaming revolution, the strikes of 2023) appears to have ascended into a triumphant recovery mode. We should all celebrate that. But here’s the danger. The blockbuster mentality as we know it kicked in during the late ’70s, and after 10 years of it, around the time Tim Burton’s “Batman” opened (launching the age of comic-book domination), there was a widespread feeling that movies, creatively, had been squeezed dry. It’s some kind of karmic poetic timing that “Batman” opened on June 23, 1989, and “Sex, Lies, and Videotape” opened less than two months later, on Aug. 18, heralding the rise of the independent-film revolution that would rescue the movie industry, much as the New Hollywood had two decades before. The indie movement meant that the blockbuster mentality would now co-exist with a different mentality. In many ways, we’re at a comparable inflection point. As a business, Hollywood has come back. “The Odyssey” is part of that — but there’s only one Christopher Nolan. The more telling success is that of the insurrectionary one-two indie-horror punch of “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” They point the way to a whole new echelon of artistic energy, coming from outside sources (like YouTube) and from a new generation. But if movies are to have a future, that generation needs to be served, and it can’t be served — and movies can’t thrive — based, simply, on the blockbuster mentality. The jackpot juggernaut of “Brand New Day” has given us amnesia about comic-book-movie fatigue; but you’d better believe it will be back. What’s needed now, more than ever, are studio executives who can serve the imperatives of the blockbuster mentality without getting fatally high on it — without forgetting that their job isn’t simply to make blockbusters.
	
	Sony Pictures, the company that released “Brand New Day,” is headed by Tom Rothman, who understands the blockbuster mentality but is also one of the last of the old-guard Hollywood executives with a track record of backing great movies that are works of popular art (like “Titanic” and “Moulin Rouge!” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood”). Will the next generation of studio heads respect and preserve the balance of those two priorities? Let’s hope so. It’s likely that the blockbuster mentality will continue to produce hits. But what it won’t produce are movies that do more than simply entertain us — movies that show us the uncanny depths of who we are. That’s the lifeblood of this art form. Without it, the blockbuster mentality is just a very hungry megaplex snake eating its own tail.

schema.headline: The Blockbuster Mentality Is Back, Baby!

title: Letterboxd Goes Down, Leaving Users Locked Out of Their Accounts
description:
Letterboxd, the cinephile social media platform for sharing movie reviews, went down Sunday morning, leaving users locked out of their accounts.

	U
body:
Letterboxd, the cinephile social media platform for sharing movie reviews, went down Sunday morning, leaving users locked out of their accounts.

	Users who opened the Letterboxd app early Sunday found themselves signed out of their profiles. Entering account information and trying to sign in causes the app to briefly load before kicking users back to the login page. When trying to sign in via the Letterboxd website, users are given the message, “An error occurred. Please try again later.”
	

	The outage began around 6 a.m. PT on Sunday, with over 1,000 users reporting issues, according to DownDetector. At the time of posting this article, the issues are ongoing. 


	Letterboxd posted the following statement on Instagram in light of the technical difficulties: “Hang in there. Our team is aware of an outage affecting service and is working to restore access as soon as possible. Thanks for your patience and support.”

	As of June, Letterboxd has more than 30 million users worldwide, adding 10 million in 2025 alone. The platform, which operates out of Auckland, New Zealand, skyrocketed in popularity during the COVID pandemic.

	A report from Puck in early July stated that Letterboxd, founded in 2011, is in early talks with a number of high-profile buyers. Interested parties allegedly include Netflix, Sony Pictures, Paramount Skydance, private equity firm TPG and Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian. Netflix, Paramount and Sony Pictures declined to comment when the report went live. Reps for TPG didn’t respond to requests for comment.

	In a statement, a Letterboxd representative said at the time: “As Letterboxd has grown, it’s natural there will be interest in what we do next. There’s nothing specific for us to share at this time. Any decision about Letterboxd’s future would involve the founders.”

schema.headline: Letterboxd Goes Down, Leaving Users Locked Out of Their Accounts

title: ‘Spring Story’ and ‘The Surubí’ Win Big at Locarno’s First Look
description: LOCARNO, Switzerland —  Cross-ocean love story “Spring Story” and false miracle comedy “The Surubí,” won big at Locarno’s 2026 pix-in-post First Loo
body:
LOCARNO, Switzerland —  Cross-ocean love story “Spring Story” and false miracle comedy “The Surubí,” won big at Locarno’s 2026 pix-in-post First Look focus on Uruguay, sharing its top five prizes at a Sunday evening Aug. 9 awards ceremony. 

	The industry plaudits went to two of the competition’s most substantial offerings, underscoring the range of productions on offer from Uruguay, also taking in an offbeat crime thriller (“Maltrato Animal”), a  historically grounded kids’ adventure (““Our Little Band of Justice”) and two auto doc-features tracing directors’ personal multi-generational family relations (“Perkal,” “The Other Side of the Net”).
	

	For director-producers Gabriela Guillermo and Irina Raffo, based out of Uruguay’s L’Avventura Cine, “Spring Story” is the case of fourth time lucky: the film No. 4 in a series of four movies set in a different season scooped both First Look’s Bright Side of the Moon prize of complete colour grading and Le Film Français Award of advertising work €5,600.  


	Germán Ormaechea’s Animista Cine co-produces.

	The most extensive of First Look’s six titles, weighing in at a rough cut of over two hours, “El Surubí” won La Mayor Cine Award, consisting of total sound post-production, and a Music Library &SFX/Acorde Award, made up of music supervision services at Music Library & SFX’s labs to a value of €45,000 ($51,750). The film also snagged a third prize, the Jannuzzi Smith Award, offering the design of an international poster worth €10,000 ($11,500).
	

	Kicking off like an Ealing or Luis Berlanga comedy, “The Surubí” is set in the post-industrial town of El Surubí, devastated by the closure of the local Pezur plant in the 1980s and now on its last legs. 

	When 70 chickens at a local farm lay 128 eggs in just one night after the arrival of a red helmet biker Emanuel, the event is described as a miracle and Emanuel hailed by the local priest as a prophet of divine powers. Whether this is true or the so called miracles can halt El Surubí’’s terminal decline is, however, another matter. 

	“El Surubí” marks the feature debut of director Lorenzo Tocco, behind “The Anniversary” (2019), a best Ibero-American short film at Guadalajara. Prominent Uruguayan prod co Monteloni produces. Brazil’s Kocria and Multiverso co-produce. 

	“’El Surubí’ is an ensemble story featuring a distinguished Uruguayan-Brazilian cast; that with humor and sensitivity, it portrays a hopeless community clinging to an illusory hope out of a need to survive,” producer Pancho Magnou Arnabal told Variety.

	A closer look at the other four First Look titles:

	“Animal Budget” (“Maltrato animal”)

	Dir. José Dell’Acqua Postiglione. Prod. José Dell’Acqua Postiglione and Germán Ormaechea (Animista Cine). 81,’ fiction

	Shot over four years, one week a year, as a showcase for not only first-time feature director but a new generation of technicians, heading key craft categories. A slow burning thriller with a quirky edge and shocks set against Uruguay’s dramatic economic crunch of 2022, “Animal Budget” turns on Javier, an animal vet drowning in debt as Uruguay’s peso plunges against the dollar and banks are closed to prevent more of a run on their funds. With no cash and literally starving, Javier starts peddling drugs and animals from his clinic. Meanwhile, an unexpected encounter, hints at a new chapter in his life.

	“Over eight years, I wrote, directed, and produced the film, seeking to blur the boundaries between fiction and reality. It is also a celebration of the talent of a new generation of Uruguayan filmmakers, many of whom took on leading creative roles in their first feature film,” told Variety.



	

					Animal Budget
	



	“The Other Side of the Net” Dir. Maximiliano Martínez Prod. Clara Charlo and Maria Zanocchi (Los Besos Contenidos), co-prod. Shoji Films (Spain) 80,’ documentary
	

	Just before flying from Montevideo to Barcelona to visit his father, Maximiliano Martínez hears him say “I love you” for the first time in 30 years. Filming him over time in Spain, Maximiliano attempts to connect. “He’s so closed,” he laments, but gradually his father opens up to his deep regret of hitting his mother. Through tennis, father and son search for a new way to reach out to each other. 

	“The film explores emotional inheritance and the possibility of transformation. What do we do with what we inherit? Are we destined to repeat it, or can we build something different?” Martínez asks, about his debut doc feature. “In this sense, ‘The Other Side of the Net’ brings a perspective that does not dive on the past, but instead seeks to project itself towards the future. It is an attempt to build relationships that are more conscious, honest, and horizontal.”



	

					The Other Side of the Net
	



	“Our Little Band of Justice” (“La pequeña Banda de la Justicia”)



	

									Lavoragine Films
	



	Dir. Guillermo Casanova 

	Prod. Natacha López Kneit (Lavorágine Films), co-prod. Lagarto Cine (Argentina) 85,’ fiction

	A kids & family departure for Casanova, behind Uruguay Oscar submissions “Seawards Journey” and “Another Story of the World,” both produced by López Kneit at their joint label Lavorágine Films, founded in 1999.  

	Set in Montevideo, 1983, as Uruguayans push for an end of dictatorship, effervescent Lucía and best friend Ana imagine they’re T-Fly and T-Splash, heroes of an American comic. Then Ana and her family suddenly disappear. Refusing to accept the adults’ silence, Lucía creates with classmates a Little Band for Justice, plastering walls with drawings demanding Ana be brought back and soon joins adults’ call for broader justice and truth. 

	“Our Little Band of Justice” tells the story of one of the darkest periods in Uruguay’s history through the eyes of children, where imagination becomes a way of understanding a world they cannot yet explain,” Casanova told Variety. 

	“Perkal”

	Dir. Paola Perkal

	Prod. Valentina Baracco Peña (Monarca Films), co-prod. Sueño Cine (Uruguay) and Insumisa Films (Spain) 75,’ documentary,”

	“’Perkal’ is a long-postponed letter to my grandmother Boke, an immigrant and war survivor,” director Paola Perkal begins the film, which tells her grandmother and father Isaac, a he decides to clear out his mother’s flat eight years after her death, taking the stash of home videos shot by Boke and Isaac for Paola. “A portrait of a family steeped in history, tradition and expectations and, says the director, “an intimate story that seeks to resignify inheritance,” said the director. “A film that clings to life and reflects on the many ways we continue to exist, even after we are gone,” added Valentina Baracco Pena, producer at Montana Films, led by Barroco and Eugenia Olascuaga Fierro. Its recent titles include “The Fable of the Turtle and the Flower,” a Sanfic 2025 premiere and “Not to Forget,”a Switzerland–Uruguay France doc-feature bowing at Visions du Réel 2023.

title: What’s It Going to Take for Steve Carell to Finally Win an Emmy?
description:
What does Steve Carell have to do for Emmy voters to take notice?

	In recent years, he’s died in car accidents twice (Apple TV’s “The Morning Show”
body:
What does Steve Carell have to do for Emmy voters to take notice?

	In recent years, he’s died in car accidents twice (Apple TV’s “The Morning Show” and Netflix’s “Four Seasons”), been a billionaire with incurable cancer (HBO’s “Mountainhead”) and a therapist held hostage by his homicidal patient (FX’s “The Patient”). Geez, hasn’t this guy been through enough?


	I guess it’s a spoiler alert, but Carell’s character on the HBO Max comedy “Rooster,” author-turned-college-instructor Greg Russo, is still alive at the end of Season 1 of the college-centric comedy. But given the recent morbid outcomes of Carell’s TV characters, it’s understandable if you held your breath and wondered if Greg would survive the season.
	

	Carell earned an Emmy nomination this year in lead actor in a comedy series for “Rooster,” which reps the star’s 12th overall nod. In the win column, however, he has a big zero. Among all of this year’s Emmy-nominated performers, Carell has the most career nominations without a win.

	That puts him in illustrious company: The only star who ever earned more Emmy nominations without a single win was “Murder She Wrote” star Angela Lansbury, who landed 18 career nominations but never won the prize before her death in 2022. (She was inducted into the Television Academy Hall of Fame in 1996, but that’s not an Emmy.)

	Somehow, Carell is now in second place among Emmy nominees without a win. His nods over the years include lead actor in a comedy series for “The Office” (as Michael Scott) in 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010 and 2011 — for every season he starred in, except the first. Carell was also nominated as a producer when “The Office” received best comedy nods in 2008, 2009, 2010 and 2011. Until this year, Carell’s last Emmy nomination was for lead actor in a drama series in 2020, via “The Morning Show.”
	

	Carell’s Emmy drought is often cited as one of the most glaring omissions of all time by Emmy voters (well, next to Lansbury — who did she have to murder to get a win?). Carell himself has been quiet about it, never really addressing the snubs in public.

	But some of his friends and colleagues have theories: Last year, director Paul Feig told Dana Carvey and David Spade on their “Fly on the Wall” podcast his theory on why Carell never won: “If you’re good, you make it look effortless.” Meanwhile, in an interview with a sports radio station in 2024, “The Office” star Creed Bratton said Carell’s lack of an Emmy was “a travesty. That’s still a bone of contention.”

	In “Rooster,” created by Bill Lawrence and Matt Tarses, Carell’s character is a successful novelist and a divorcé whose relationship with his daughter, Katie (Charly Clive), is complicated. It gets even more complex when he winds up getting a job as a visiting lecturer at the small New England college where Katie also teaches. The show plays to Carell’s strengths, both in awkward comedy (Greg is a bit of a mess) and in touching, dramatic moments as he connects with his daughter and his new colleagues.

	But breaking his Emmy losing streak is going to be tough. For one thing, Carell’s is the only Emmy nomination for “Rooster,” and he faces tough competition from “Widow’s Bay” star Matthew Rhys. Others in the category include “Only Murders in the Building” star Martin Short, “Wonder Man” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II (whose show was just shockingly and disappointingly canceled) and the star of Lawrence’s “Shrinking” juggernaut, Jason Segel.

	And perhaps just as telling, Carell hasn’t been campaigning for this Emmy. There’s an ongoing debate over how much hitting the trail matters — but especially in a race like this, you’ve got to shake a few hands and snap a few selfies. Without that, Carell is likely to have to settle for a hopefully luckier Emmy nomination No. 13.

title: Florian Hoffmann’s U.N. Compound Drama ‘Yazz’ Takes Main Alliance 4 Development Prizes at Locarno Pro Awards
description: Florian Hoffmann’s “Yazz,” about a teenager growing up in a UN compound in the Central African Republic, celebrated two major wins at this year’s Lo
body:
Florian Hoffmann’s “Yazz,” about a teenager growing up in a UN compound in the Central African Republic, celebrated two major wins at this year’s Locarno Pro Awards for the Alliance 4 Development co-development platform for projects from Austria, France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland

	Swiss-German-French co-production from Tellfilm, NiKo Film and Eaux Vives Productions beat out 10 other projects for top prizes. “Yazz” took home both the Nebel Studios Award, estimated at CHF 30,500 ($37,678) for three days of studio use and five days of camera equipment, and the Studio13/Valais Film Commission Award, estimated at close to $14,825 for five days of studio use at Studio13 in Valais, Switzerland.
	

	“What really struck us about ‘Yazz’ is its unique and very personal perspective on a world we think we know, but rarely see from the inside,” the jury stated. “The project has also shown to be at incredibly advanced stage of development that has already received strong recognition, with experienced co-production partners on board, great talent attached and development funding secured in Switzerland — confirming our belief in the project’s artistic and production potential.”


	The Masé Studios Post-Production Award, worth nearly $31,000 in post-production services, was shared by queer and feminist coming-of-age musical “Cuore Matto,” by Tamer Ruggli, produced by Francine Lusser and Gérard Monier of Switzerland’s Tipimages Productions, and “Les Orages Magnétiques” (“Magnetic Storms”) by Wendy Pillonel, produced by Flavia Zanon of Swiss shingle Close Up Films, a coming-of-age tale that explores the complexity of becoming a woman in a misogynistic environment. “Les Orages Magnétiques”also picked up the Midpoint Consulting Award, an online script consultancy with a Midpoint Institute expert.
	

	“Sparare alle Angurie”(“Shooting Watermelons”) by Antonio Donato, produced by Santiago Fondevila Sancet at Italy’s Cinedora, received the Masé Studios Award, a cash voucher worth more than $3,706. The story centers on an authoritarian father and his two sons on vacation following a difficult separation and explores themes of power, masculinity and patriarchy.

	Jessica Puppo’s “Le Règne des Silures”(“Reign of Silures”), produced by Alexis Perrin (Rumble Fish Productions, France), won the Ticino Film Commission Residence Award: a two-day location scout worth nearly $5,000 plus a letter of intent for financial support up to CHF 12,000 ($14,824) should the film shoot in Ticino.

	Bruce LaBruce’s “Third Take,” produced by Nicolas Brevière (Local Films, France), took the Alphapanda Market Breakout Award consisting of consultancy services worth some $4,320.

	Heritage Restoration Contest

	Since 2022, in collaboration with the Zurich-based Cinegrell film lab, the Locarno Film Festival’s Heritage Restoration Contest has been dedicated to bringing cinematic heritage back to life.

	This year’s prize went to 1997’s “Nous sommes tous encore ici” (“We’re All Still Here”) by Anne-Marie Miéville, a three-part meditation on philosophy and everyday life featuring Jean-Luc Godard in a rare on-screen role.

	It was selected by an international jury composed of Amy Homma, director and president of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection; Leslie Vuchot, CEO and founder of The Festival Agency; and Nicole T. Allemann, head of film restoration and lab at Zurich-based post-production group Cinegrell.

	As part of the award, the film will undergo a complete restoration at Cinegrell and then premiere at the 2027 edition of the festival.

	“First presented at the festival in 1997, ‘Nous sommes tous encore ici’ is an essential work of Swiss cinema by one of the country’s leading female directors,” the jury said. “In the year of its 30th anniversary, this restoration offers a long-overdue opportunity to rediscover both the film and the work of a major filmmaker, whose contribution to Swiss cinema deserves renewed recognition, as Locarno approaches its 80th edition.”

	Now in its fourth edition, the Heritage Restoration Contest previously honored “Letter From My Village” (1976) by Safi Faye; “The Cannibals”(1969) by Liliana Cavani; and Mulher de Verdade(1954) by Alberto Cavalcanti.

title: NBA Legend Don Nelson Dead at 86, Family Announces
description:
NBA Legend Don Nelson
                          Dead at 86
body:
NBA Legend Don Nelson
                          Dead at 86
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 9, 2026
                            11:11 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Five-time NBA champion and Hall of Fame coach Don Nelson has died at 86, his family announced Sunday.
      
    
            Nelson’s family announced his death Sunday, saying the Basketball Hall of Famer passed away peacefully surrounded by loved ones ... saying "On Sunday morning our beloved husband, dad, grandfather and great-grandfather Don Nelson peacefully went to be with the Lord, surrounded by his loving family."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            They added ... "Throughout his last week, friends and family encircled him with love, sharing the blessing of his friendship and revisiting treasured memories." A cause of death was not mentioned.
      

            Nelson built a legendary career both on the court and from the sidelines. As a player, he won five NBA championships with the Boston Celtics during his 14-year playing career. He later transitioned into coaching, where he became one of the winningest coaches in league history.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nelson coached the Milwaukee Bucks, Golden State Warriors, New York Knicks and Dallas Mavericks, collecting 1,335 regular-season victories during his coaching career. He was named NBA Coach of the Year three times and was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2012.
      
    
            Nelson was known for his unconventional approach to basketball and was considered an innovator who helped popularize smaller lineups and creative offensive strategies. His time with Golden State produced some of the NBA’s most entertaining teams, while his tenure in Dallas helped shape the careers of stars including Dirk Nowitzki and Steve Nash.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In 2025, Nelson received the Chuck Daly Lifetime Achievement Award, further cementing his place among the sport’s coaching legends.
      
    
            Nelson leaves behind an enormous basketball legacy ... but to his family, he was first and foremost a husband, father, grandfather and great-grandfather.

schema.headline: NBA Legend Don Nelson Dead at 86, Family Announces
